title: When Your CRM Starts Building Itself: The CIO’s Role in the Agentic SaaS Era
gist: Agentic AI lets business users build and run their own CRM agents without IT, and BCG argues that within a couple of years large enterprises will run hundreds to thousands of agents that make pricing, lead-prioritization and outreach decisions at machine speed. The CIO's response should be to stop owning delivery and instead own four foundations — data architecture, agent governance, an enterprise-controlled orchestration layer, and the cost model — as SaaS pricing shifts from seats to consumption.

insights.claim: Every major enterprise SaaS platform now ships with capabilities that let business users build and automate their own CRM workflows without deep technical expertise or day-to-day reliance on IT, so the open question is adoption timing rather than availability.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The capability overhang is already shipped and paid for; a step-change in usage can arrive without any new product cycle, which front-loads both consumption revenue for SaaS vendors and governance spend for buyers.
insights.quote: Every major enterprise SaaS platform now ships with capabilities that put more control in the hands of business users. The question is when they will start to use them.
insights.locator: CRM development is becoming a lot more democratic

insights.claim: AI agents differ from prior citizen-development waves such as Access databases, SharePoint and low-code apps because agents do not merely present information — they make decisions, execute them, and incur cost with every action.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Governance tooling built for document and app sprawl does not transfer; budget for a new category of agent registry, audit and spend controls.
insights.quote: But AI agents change the equation because they don’t just present information. They make decisions, act on them, and run up costs with every action they take.
insights.locator: CIOs have seen citizen development before

insights.claim: Seventy percent of technology leaders say their business teams are deploying technology faster than IT can track, meaning the visibility gap predates agentic AI rather than being created by it.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Shadow-IT discovery and agent-inventory tooling faces demand from a majority of enterprises immediately, not after a long education cycle.
insights.quote: Already, 70% of technology leaders say that their business teams are deploying technology faster than IT can track.
insights.locator: Already, 70% of technology leaders say

insights.claim: More than half of sellers have already used AI agents and nearly nine in ten expect to by 2027, according to Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales report.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sales is the beachhead function for agent adoption; watch Salesforce consumption disclosures as the cleanest read on real agentic usage versus announced usage.
insights.quote: More than half of sellers have used agents, according to Salesforce’s 2026 State of Sales report, and nearly nine in ten expect to do so by 2027.
insights.locator: The pressure to open up development will only increase

insights.claim: Among sales leaders at organizations already using agents, 94% say agents are critical to meeting business demands, indicating that early deployments are becoming load-bearing rather than experimental.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Once agents are described as critical, budgets become defensive and hard to cut — supportive of recurring agentic SaaS revenue durability.
insights.quote: Among sales leaders whose organizations already use them, 94% say that agents are critical to meeting business demands.
insights.locator: More than half of sellers have used agents

insights.claim: Within a couple of years a large enterprise can reasonably expect to run hundreds of agents and in some cases thousands, a scale few technology leaders are currently prepared to manage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Agent count per enterprise is the unit that drives consumption billing, observability spend and identity/permissioning demand — a multi-order-of-magnitude TAM expansion versus seats.
insights.quote: Within a couple of years, a large enterprise can reasonably expect to be running hundreds of agents, and in some cases thousands.
insights.locator: As reliance on agents grows

insights.claim: Enterprises are already discovering dozens of ungoverned AI agents running across sales and service functions that make decisions about pricing, lead prioritization and customer outreach before any tracking framework exists.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Ungoverned pricing agents are a live audit and disclosure risk; expect discovery-and-inventory products to sell before governance platforms do.
insights.quote: enterprises discover dozens of ungoverned AI agents running across sales and service functions, making decisions about pricing, lead prioritization, and customer outreach before any framework exists to track them
insights.locator: We are starting to see how this will play out

themes.theme: Why CRM has the largest blast radius

insights.claim: CRM is the highest-stakes venue for agentic building because it sits at the intersection of the customer record, revenue-critical workflows and customer trust, so a misfiring agent can damage data, revenue and trust simultaneously.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: CRM vendors capture the most agentic value and carry the most tail risk; governance failures there are the likeliest source of a headline incident that resets buyer expectations.
insights.quote: the customer record, revenue-critical workflows, and customer trust
insights.locator: That gap matters across the technology landscape

insights.claim: When functions build agents independently they create divergent definitions of basic concepts — sales and service may each define an "active customer" differently — fragmenting the single customer record and rippling into billing, forecasting, analytics and compliance.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Definition drift shows up first in forecast quality and billing disputes — a leading indicator to probe in earnings calls of heavy agent adopters.
insights.quote: different parts of the business begin operating from different versions of the truth
insights.locator: The customer record fragments

insights.claim: Agents that can prioritize leads, recommend discounts and generate offers convert what were once human judgment calls into machine-speed execution, so without autonomy limits a single bad decision becomes a bad decision at scale — for example a renewal agent applying an unapproved discount across hundreds of accounts before anyone spots the pattern.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Uncontrolled agent discounting is a direct margin and net-revenue-retention leak; approval thresholds on agent pricing authority are the control to ask about.
insights.quote: A renewal agent that applies an unapproved discount, for example, could affect hundreds of accounts before anyone spots the pattern.
insights.locator: Agents make revenue decisions without adequate controls

insights.claim: Every additional agent built inside a SaaS platform ties more enterprise workflow to that vendor, and the resulting lock-in is commercial as much as technical because rising switching costs directly reduce the customer's negotiating leverage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Agent counts inside a vendor's platform are a forward indicator of pricing power and renewal uplift for that vendor — bullish for incumbent platform economics, bearish for buyer budgets.
insights.quote: As the cost of switching rises, the enterprise’s negotiating leverage falls, too.
insights.locator: Vendor lock-in gets deeper

themes.theme: Why agentic programs die — management, not models

insights.claim: Many agentic programs are being abandoned before reaching production for recurring reasons: costs outrun the business case, teams lack a baseline for comparing value, and IT bolts risk controls onto existing systems instead of designing them in — failures of management rather than of the models.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Pilot-to-production attrition is an organizational bottleneck, so better frontier models alone will not convert enterprise AI pilots into revenue — a caution on bullish enterprise-AI conversion assumptions.
insights.quote: These are management failures, not model failures.
insights.locator: The stakes are becoming clear

insights.claim: Re-centralizing agent development fails either way: business teams will queue or route around the process, and requiring IT sign-off on every agent simply trades a development bottleneck for a governance bottleneck.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Policy-as-code and guardrail tooling wins over approval-workflow tooling; bet on controls that run inline rather than review boards.
insights.quote: That approach trades a development bottleneck for a governance bottleneck.
insights.locator: Own the Foundations, Not the Delivery

insights.claim: The governing design principle is to balance control with velocity by making the safe path the fastest path, so that distributed building expands innovation capacity because every user becomes a potential builder.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Adoption accrues to platforms whose guardrails reduce friction rather than add steps — a product differentiator to test in agent platform evaluations.
insights.quote: balancing control with velocity to make the safe path the fastest path
insights.locator: Avoiding them means balancing control with velocity

themes.theme: The four foundations CIOs should own

insights.claim: CIOs should stop owning delivery on the platform and instead own four foundations — the data architecture, the agent governance model, the orchestration layer, and the cost model underpinning commercial strategy — while business functions own use cases, agents and outcomes.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: This is the emerging enterprise buying blueprint: four distinct budget lines (data/identity, governance, orchestration, FinOps) rather than one agent platform purchase.
insights.quote: Stop owning delivery on the platform and start owning the foundations: the data architecture, the agent governance model, the orchestration layer, and the cost model underpinning the commercial strategy.
insights.locator: So what should CIOs do?

insights.claim: Customer data must be made agent-ready rather than report-ready: report-ready data answers what happened, while agent-ready data must answer what an agent is allowed to do, for whom, right now.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Permissions-and-entitlements context, not analytics warehousing, is the data layer agents need — a different spend category from BI and a tailwind for identity/entitlement infrastructure.
insights.quote: Report-ready data answers “What happened?” Agent-ready data must answer “What am I allowed to do, and for whom, right now?”
insights.locator: Data Architecture: Give Every Agent the Same Truth

insights.claim: Agent autonomy should be earned in graduated, revocable steps — from recommending actions for human approval, to acting independently in limited cases, to full autonomy within a defined scope — with autonomy reduced when an agent degrades or breaches its boundaries.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Graduated autonomy implies slower-than-hyped removal of human labor from workflows; headcount displacement lags agent deployment.
insights.quote: Autonomy should be earned in graduated, revocable steps.
insights.locator: Agent Governance Model: Make Agents Earn Their Autonomy

insights.claim: Every agent needs a named accountable human owner plus full lifecycle management — registration, monitoring, review as it changes, retirement when value fades — with audit trails, decision logs, cost and performance tracking, behavior alerts and a tested kill switch as standard.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Defines the feature checklist for agent-ops platforms; a tested kill switch and per-agent cost tracking are the items most current tooling lacks.
insights.quote: Audit trails, decision logs, cost and performance tracking, alerts for unexpected behavior, and a tested kill switch should be standard parts of the model.
insights.locator: Agents require governance and oversight throughout their life cycle

themes.theme: Orchestration as the strategic control point

insights.claim: Because enterprises will rarely rely on a single agent provider, the orchestration layer that decides which agent or platform handles a task becomes the strategic control point, and the CIO must deliberately decide whether the CRM vendor controls it or merely participates in it rather than letting the answer emerge by default.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Ownership of orchestration is where durable enterprise AI value accrues — a contested layer between CRM incumbents, hyperscalers and independent orchestration vendors.
insights.quote: The orchestration layer serves as a strategic control point that determines which agent or platform handles a task and how work moves between agents or platforms.
insights.locator: Enterprise-Controlled Orchestration Layer

insights.claim: Retaining the ability to route work to a different model, agent or provider preserves commercial leverage as well as technical flexibility: the easier it is to move work elsewhere, the less the enterprise depends on any single vendor.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Portability erodes model and platform pricing power over time — an argument against assuming permanent premium pricing for any single frontier model in enterprise workloads.
insights.quote: That flexibility preserves commercial leverage, too: the easier it is to move work elsewhere, the less the enterprise must depend on any single vendor.
insights.locator: The goal is to preserve choice

insights.claim: The proposed stress test for lock-in is how much of the agent estate could move to an alternative platform within six months if the CRM provider changed its pricing model tomorrow.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A usable diligence metric for gauging how much pricing power a SaaS incumbent actually holds over its agentic installed base.
insights.quote: If the CRM provider changed its pricing model tomorrow, how much of the agent estate could move to an alternative platform within six months?
insights.locator: A simple test: If the CRM provider changed its pricing model

insights.claim: Agentic SaaS is shifting software economics from predictable seat-based licenses toward charging for usage, actions or outcomes, with most major SaaS vendors having already layered an AI consumption meter on top of existing seat pricing.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Revenue per customer decouples from headcount — model SaaS growth off agent activity, and expect reported revenue volatility to rise as consumption mix grows.
insights.quote: Most major SaaS vendors have already layered an AI consumption meter on top of existing seat pricing (while also bundling AI capabilities into new SKUs that carry a step-up at renewal).
insights.locator: Consumption costs run away

insights.claim: Vendors are simultaneously bundling AI capabilities into new SKUs that carry a step-up at renewal, so buyers face both a metered charge and a higher list price at contract reset.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Renewal step-ups are a quiet second lever on SaaS ARPU beyond headline consumption — watch renewal cohorts rather than new logos for the real price increase.
insights.locator: Consumption costs run away

insights.claim: A single high-volume agent running automated outreach or resolving customer cases can incur costs at a pace bearing little resemblance to headcount-based budgeting, and independent team building removes the natural budget ceilings that traditional licenses provided.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect bill-shock episodes and subsequent FinOps-for-agents demand; unbudgeted overages can produce lumpy vendor revenue followed by customer pushback.
insights.quote: The result can be a very unwelcome surprise when the bill arrives.
insights.locator: Consumption costs run away

insights.claim: A listed cost per seat tells you little once agent activity drives the bill, so the useful unit of measure becomes cost per business result such as a resolved case or a qualified lead.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Cost-per-outcome becomes the enterprise software KPI that replaces cost-per-seat — reframing how software budgets and vendor comparisons are built.
insights.quote: A listed cost per seat tells you little when agent activity drives the bill.
insights.locator: Cost Model: Make the Economics Visible

insights.claim: Charging agent consumption back to the function that built the agent is what creates real accountability for both cost and delivered value.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Chargeback introduces internal demand elasticity for agent usage — a dampener on the consumption-revenue growth assumptions vendors are modeling.
insights.quote: Charging consumption back to the function brings that accountability home.
insights.locator: The function that builds an agent should be accountable

insights.claim: Armed with outcome economics, CIOs can shift vendor negotiation away from seats and discounts toward challenging pricing on the economics of the outcomes the technology delivers, and should scrutinize contract fine print on what generates a charge, whether rates stay predictable as consumption changes, and whether workloads can be moved elsewhere.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: As buyers professionalize on consumption contracts, expect pressure on vendor take rates and more rate-cap and portability clauses in renewals.
insights.locator: The same information will strengthen the CIO’s hand with vendors

insights.claim: The cost-model readiness test is whether the CIO can tell the CFO today what each AI agent costs per business outcome; identifying the spending without knowing what it delivered means the economics are not yet managed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Most enterprises will fail this test today, implying a near-term wave of agent FinOps spend and, potentially, agent program cancellations once true unit costs surface.
insights.quote: Is it possible to tell the CFO today what each AI agent costs per business outcome?
insights.locator: A simple test: Is it possible to tell the CFO

insights.claim: Most enterprises have more agents running than they are aware of, so the first move is a function-by-function inventory of everything built on the CRM stack, giving every agent an identity and a named owner.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Agent identity is emerging as a distinct infrastructure category alongside human IAM; discovery is the wedge product.
insights.quote: CIOs cannot govern what they cannot see.
insights.locator: Inventory what exists

insights.claim: Within the next year the agent estate could outgrow many enterprises' ability to track it, and the governance work is far easier on a cohort of 50 agents than on a cohort of 500.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sets a roughly 12-month window for agent governance purchases; vendors selling into that window should see demand pull forward in 2026-2027.
insights.quote: This work is far easier to perform on a cohort of 50 agents than on a cohort of 500.
insights.locator: The clock is ticking
